title: How it works
use_cases: Use when developing a narrative framework to ensure genre-specific commitments are met
Configure when designing inciting premises and escalation patterns for fiction writing
Implement when structuring plot reversals that align with reader expectations for mystery or romance
Use when evaluating internal consistency and load-bearing world-building logic
content:
Genre fiction operates through a system of promises and payoffs. The genre label on the cover is a promise; the story's execution either delivers or violates that promise. Violating it is not automatically bad — sometimes subversion is the whole point — but a writer who does it without awareness usually just confuses readers.

The mechanics vary by genre, but most operate through 4 structural commitments:

1. An inciting premise that establishes the genre's core tension — a crime, a magical system, a romantic meet, a threat to civilization.
2. Genre-specific escalation patterns — mystery tightens its net of suspects; romance builds emotional intimacy through conflict; fantasy escalates the cost of magic.
3. Midpoint reversal or complication that raises the stakes in a genre-appropriate way (the wrong suspect in mystery; the central couple separating in romance; the mentor's death in epic fantasy).
4. A genre-mandatory resolution — mystery solves, romance unites, thriller neutralizes the threat.

World-building is particularly load-bearing in fantasy and science fiction. A poorly constructed magic system creates plot holes; a poorly constructed romance arc creates emotional incoherence. The internal logic of the genre's fictional reality has to be consistent enough that readers feel the rules are real — even when those rules involve dragons.
